description: Connector-layer authorization vectors for Solana user decryption: the host policy applied to a request against a recorded observation of host state.

deployment.chain_id_derivation: deployment-time rule: chain_id = be_u64(0x01 || genesis_hash[0..7]), applied once per cluster and configured everywhere. Nothing in the authorization path recomputes it, so this set's pair is a synthetic cluster: the chain id below is not the rule applied to the genesis hash below, and no check reads the genesis hash at all. Vectors for the rule itself live with the permit fixtures.

vectors.name: direct
vectors.comment: The reference request: the signer names a handle they were allowed on, the leaf record serves the allow leaf, it verifies against the encrypted store's peaks, and the account's (program, scope) is in the signed scopes.

vectors.name: delegated
vectors.comment: A handle the delegator was allowed on, used by the signer under a live delegation for the encrypted store's authority. The allowed key is the delegator.

vectors.name: delegated-via-wildcard-row
vectors.comment: A delegator grants across every authority of theirs with one row carrying the reserved sentinel instead of an encrypted store authority. It authorizes an encrypted value account that has no authority-specific row, exactly as the EVM ACL's wildcard delegation does. The consequence is part of the rule: revoking the authority-specific row does not stop a delegate who holds this one.

vectors.name: allowed-then-handle-replaced
vectors.comment: The handle has been replaced since the signer was allowed on it, and the request still authorizes: the allow leaf names the handle, and a write to the account seals nothing about the handles before it. There is no current-handle rule.

vectors.name: leaf-record-behind-by-a-non-merging-append
vectors.comment: The leaf record has sealed one leaf fewer than the observation shows, and the append it missed left the proof's peak alone, so the proof it serves still verifies. Age alone is not a failure: rejecting this would fail every request that raced a write.

vectors.name: permissive-scope-foreign-application
vectors.comment: An empty signed scope list is permissive: the scope rule is skipped entirely, so an encrypted store of any application is in scope. The allow leaf still has to exist.

vectors.name: duplicate-handle
vectors.comment: Naming the same handle twice is legal: each occurrence counts toward the budget, is authorized independently, and is bound at its own position by the response. The leaf record is asked once for the one leaf.

vectors.name: mixed-direct-and-two-delegators
vectors.comment: One request freely mixes a direct entry with entries from two different delegators. There is no per-request mode and no separate delegated route.

vectors.name: delegated-one-authority-spans-scopes
vectors.comment: A single delegation row authorizes the delegator's values in two different scopes: the row is keyed by (delegator, delegate, encrypted store authority) and the scope is not among the PDA's seeds. The signed scopes still have to name both — that is the permit's rule, not the delegation's.

vectors.name: many-handles-in-one-request
vectors.comment: One request naming many handles from one encrypted store. No layer of the Connector caps the count: the system-wide decryption budget is summed and enforced by the Gateway entry point on chain, so a request that exists has already passed it.

vectors.name: absent-invalidation-record
vectors.comment: A user who has never revoked anything has no invalidation record, and its absence reads as a watermark of zero rather than as a missing initialisation step.

vectors.name: prefunded-invalidation-address
vectors.comment: The invalidation address of a user who has never revoked, holding the account a bare transfer leaves behind: System-program-owned and empty. Every address in this path is derivable by anyone, so this is the same "the host program never wrote here" observation as no account at all, and it is not the user's choice which of the two they are presented as. An implementation that reads it any other way sells a terminal denial of a user's every request for the price of one transfer.

vectors.name: future-start-permit-outliving-a-revocation
vectors.comment: The permit's window opens after a revocation that was performed before it opened, so the revocation does not reach it and the request is authorized. This is a recorded weakness of the watermark design, accepted for parity with the EVM path and filed as a follow-up for both — not a property this set endorses.

vectors.name: wrong-host-program
vectors.comment: A permit signed for another host program authorizes nothing here, even on the right cluster.
vectors.mutation: the permit's verifying program id is replaced with another program

vectors.name: wrong-host-chain-id
vectors.comment: A permit signed for another cluster authorizes nothing here, even under the same program id — which is why the cluster is signed at all.
vectors.mutation: the permit's chain id, and the chain id embedded in its handle, name another cluster

vectors.name: mixed-embedded-chain-ids
vectors.comment: Handles of one request must embed one chain id. A mixed batch is refused rather than resolved by taking the first handle as the truth.
vectors.mutation: a second entry is appended whose handle embeds another cluster

vectors.name: handle-of-another-cluster
vectors.comment: Handles agreeing among themselves is not enough: every embedded chain id must equal the signed one, or the request is about another cluster's ciphertexts.
vectors.mutation: the entry's handle embeds another cluster while the permit still names this one

vectors.name: expired-permit
vectors.comment: The validity window has closed. No later observation makes a permit younger.
vectors.mutation: the request is authorized after the permit's window ends

vectors.name: not-yet-valid-permit
vectors.comment: The window has not opened. Transient, because this is the one rejection that the passage of time repairs on its own.
vectors.mutation: the request is authorized before the permit's window starts

vectors.name: invalidated-permit
vectors.comment: The permit started before its signer's last revocation, so it is dead permanently. This is the mechanism behind revoking every outstanding signature with one transaction.
vectors.mutation: the signer's invalidation record holds a watermark above the permit's start

vectors.name: invalidation-record-of-another-user
vectors.comment: The invalidation record's contents are checked against the address it was read from: a record naming another user is refused rather than read as that user's watermark, and refused rather than read as zero.
vectors.mutation: the signer's invalidation address holds a record naming a different user

vectors.name: host-paused
vectors.comment: The operator paused the host. User decryption is served entirely by the Connector, so the pause switch reaches it only through this rule — without it a paused deployment would keep releasing plaintext while refusing every on-chain write. Transient: the permit and the handles survive the pause, so the same request authorizes once the operator lifts it.
vectors.mutation: the deployment's config singleton carries paused = true

vectors.name: destroyed-kms-epoch
vectors.comment: Governance destroyed the epoch the permit signed. Transient, and deliberately so: the Connector learns about the pair from a single boolean that is true only when the epoch is active and belongs to the signed context, so a destroyed epoch is indistinguishable from one that is not active yet. The request is retried within the attempt budget and never succeeds — inherited behaviour of the pair validation the EVM path shares, not a decision of the Solana path, and fail-closed either way.
vectors.mutation: the KMS management state reports the signed epoch as destroyed

vectors.name: not-yet-active-kms-epoch
vectors.comment: The epoch exists but is not active yet. The reference case of the transient outcome, and the reason the two records around it share both its rule and its recoverability: all three arrive as the same boolean.
vectors.mutation: the KMS management state reports the signed epoch as not active yet

vectors.name: kms-epoch-of-another-context
vectors.comment: The signed epoch belongs to a different context, so the pair will never be servable — and it is transient for the same reason as the destroyed epoch: the view returns one boolean, and no view exposes the epoch's context on its own.
vectors.mutation: the KMS management state reports the signed epoch as belonging to another context

vectors.name: empty-handle-list
vectors.comment: A request naming no handles has nothing to authorize and nothing for a response to bind.
vectors.mutation: the handle list is emptied

vectors.name: handle-list-past-the-cap
vectors.comment: Every rule is evaluated against one atomic account snapshot, and a standard RPC node serves at most 100 accounts per call — in the worst case three per entry plus the signer's invalidation record, so the list is capped at 33. The Gateway refuses a longer request at admission, before the fee; the Connector rejects it too, so the snapshot's readability is its own invariant rather than an assumption about the contract upstream. Duplicates count: the cap is on the list, not on the distinct handles in it.
vectors.mutation: the live handle is repeated until the list is one entry past the cap

vectors.name: missing-encrypted-value-account
vectors.comment: The encrypted store does not exist at this observation. Transient by nature: the account may simply not have reached the observed commitment yet.
vectors.mutation: the encrypted store is removed from the observation

vectors.name: encrypted-value-account-owned-by-another-program
vectors.comment: Program ownership is the sole trust anchor: an account with impeccable contents under another program's ownership proves nothing.
vectors.mutation: the encrypted store's owner is replaced with another program

vectors.name: delegation-record-as-encrypted-value-account
vectors.comment: A host-owned account of another type is caught by the discriminator rather than by what its bytes happen to mean when read as an encrypted store.
vectors.mutation: the encrypted store address holds a delegation record instead

vectors.name: encrypted-value-account-with-a-truncated-body
vectors.comment: A body cut short is not the same thing as a body followed by extra bytes: the first cannot be read, the second is an account with room to spare.
vectors.mutation: eight bytes are removed from the end of the encrypted store

vectors.name: encrypted-value-account-at-another-address
vectors.comment: The account's own fields must derive the address it was read from. This is the backstop that makes a substituted encrypted store a rejection rather than a redirection.
vectors.mutation: the encrypted store address holds an encrypted store of another authority

vectors.name: handle-of-an-unsigned-scope
vectors.comment: With a non-empty signed scope list, every entry's encrypted store must have its (program, scope) in it. The pair tested is the account's — a request has no field for it.
vectors.mutation: the entry names an encrypted store whose scope is outside the signed scopes

vectors.name: key-never-allowed
vectors.comment: The only allow leaf on the handle names somebody else, and the leaf record has the chain's whole history: the signer was never allowed, and repeating the request changes nothing.
vectors.mutation: the encrypted store's allow leaf names another key

vectors.name: handle-never-allowed-to-the-key
vectors.comment: Being allowed on the handle the account used to hold says nothing about the one it holds now: access is per handle, and each handle needs its own leaf.
vectors.mutation: the request names the replacement handle, which no leaf allows

vectors.name: leaf-record-behind-without-the-leaf
vectors.comment: The observation shows one leaf and the record has sealed none: the record is behind, and its answer says nothing about the leaf yet. Retryable — the record catches up.
vectors.mutation: the leaf record has not sealed the append that holds the allow leaf

vectors.name: leaf-record-unknown-account
vectors.comment: The chain has the account and the record has never seen it: the record has not indexed the account's creation yet. Retryable for the same reason as a record behind.
vectors.mutation: the encrypted store is unknown to the leaf record

vectors.name: leaf-history-incomplete
vectors.comment: The record's history for the account has a gap it cannot close. It can prove nothing about the account until rebuilt, and no retry within a request's budget rebuilds it.
vectors.mutation: the leaf record reports its history for the account as incomplete

vectors.name: leaf-record-ahead-of-the-observation
vectors.comment: The record has sealed a leaf this observation does not have yet. There is nothing for the proof to be a proof of, and it is refused before any hashing. Retryable: the same request authorizes once the observation catches up.
vectors.mutation: the observation holds an earlier state than the one the record has sealed

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-for-another-encrypted-value-account
vectors.comment: A leaf sealed for another encrypted store authorizes nothing here.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to another encrypted store

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-for-another-key
vectors.comment: A leaf sealed for another key authorizes only that key.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to another key

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-for-another-handle
vectors.comment: A leaf sealed for another handle authorizes only that handle.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to another handle

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-at-another-position
vectors.comment: A leaf whose committed position is not the position it occupies authorizes nothing.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to leaf index one while occupying index zero

vectors.name: public-decrypt-leaf-as-allow-leaf
vectors.comment: Public decryptability is a separate flow with its own leaf domain. Its leaf says nothing about any key and must not double as evidence that one was allowed.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf is a public-decrypt leaf rather than an allow leaf

vectors.name: leaf-record-behind-by-a-merging-append
vectors.comment: The record is one append behind and the append merged the proof's peak, so the sibling path it serves no longer reaches any peak the observation holds. Retryable: once the record catches up it serves the longer path, and the same request authorizes.
vectors.mutation: the append the record has not sealed merges the leaf's peak

vectors.name: missing-delegation
vectors.comment: No delegation record at the canonical address for the tuple, so the delegated entry has nothing standing behind it. Transient, not terminal: a grant confirmed on another RPC is simply not here yet for a reader sitting at an earlier confirmed slot, and refusing it terminally would fail a valid request permanently over ordinary replica lag.
vectors.mutation: the delegation record is removed from the observation

vectors.name: revoked-delegation
vectors.comment: The delegator revoked it. Subsequent requests stop immediately, while the signer's own permit remains valid — two independent levers, one per party.
vectors.mutation: the delegation record is marked revoked

vectors.name: expired-delegation
vectors.comment: Expiry is measured against the observed slot, not against a local clock.
vectors.mutation: the delegation's expiration slot falls below the observed slot

vectors.name: delegation-newer-than-the-observation
vectors.comment: A record written after the observation is not part of the state this authorization saw. Accepting it would mean authorizing from two points in time at once. Transient, not terminal: the record's last update slot comes from the on-chain clock and the observed slot is the response's own context slot, so a coherent node cannot produce this, and it reports an incoherent observation rather than a dead grant. A repeat against a coherent node authorizes.
vectors.mutation: the delegation's last update slot is above the observed slot

vectors.name: delegation-record-of-another-tuple
vectors.comment: A record sitting at the canonical address while naming a different tuple is refused: the address alone is not taken as proof of what the record says.
vectors.mutation: the delegation address holds a record naming another delegator

vectors.name: delegation-record-naming-another-delegate
vectors.comment: The delegate half of the tuple rule: a record at the canonical address delegating to somebody else is refused. Sitting at the address derived from the delegate is not taken as proof of naming them.
vectors.mutation: the delegation address holds a record naming another delegate

vectors.name: delegation-record-owned-by-another-program
vectors.comment: Only the host program grants delegations; an account under another program's ownership is not one.
vectors.mutation: the delegation record's owner is replaced with another program

vectors.name: encrypted-value-account-record-as-delegation
vectors.comment: A host-owned account of another type at the delegation address is caught by its discriminator, the mirror of the same substitution against an encrypted store.
vectors.mutation: the delegation address holds an encrypted store instead

vectors.name: no-live-delegation-row
vectors.comment: The delegator holds both an authority-specific row and a wildcard row, and both are revoked. The rejection names both reasons: either row could have authorized this entry on its own, so naming one of them would describe half of the state the delegate has to fix.
vectors.mutation: both the authority-specific and the wildcard delegation rows are marked revoked

vectors.name: sentinel-authority-in-the-encrypted-value-account
vectors.comment: An encrypted store naming the wildcard sentinel as its authority is rejected at resolution, before any delegation row is read. A live wildcard row is present — exactly the row a sentinel authority would resolve to — so an implementation without this guard authorizes the request, with its authority-specific check structurally a wildcard check.
vectors.mutation: the encrypted store names the wildcard sentinel as its authority
